 On some upper bounds on the intersection number of a finite
                      soluble group

 A. Ballester-Bolinches , R.V. Borodich, and S.F. Kamornikov


     Abstract. For a ﬁnite group G, the intersection number α(G) of G is the
     minimal number of maximal subgroups of G whose intersection coincides
     with Φ(G), the Frattini subgroup of G. In this paper, new upper bounds
     on α(G) are established when G is soluble.

     Mathematics Subject Classification. 20D10, 20D20, 20D35.

     Keywords. Finite soluble group, Maximal subgroup, Frattini subgroup,
     Intersection number.




1. Introduction. All groups considered in this paper are ﬁnite.
   If G is a group, following [5] (see also [10]), we denote by α(G) the minimal
number of maximal subgroups of G whose intersection coincides with Φ(G);
α(G) is called the intersection number of G (see [1]).
   Let λ(G) be the number of chief factors in a given chief series of a group
G. The following upper bound was shown in [5].

Theorem 1 ([5, Theorem 3]). If G is a soluble group, then α(G) ≤ λ(G).

    Let F (G) denote the Fitting subgroup of G, that is, the largest nilpotent
normal subgroup of G. The following upper bound of α(G) was obtained in
[8]. Since this paper is written in Russian, we consider it convenient to include
the proof of that result here for the sake of completeness.

Theorem 2 ([8, Theorem 1.1]). Let G be a soluble group. Assume that n is the
length of a given G-chief series of the group F (G)/Φ(G), and k is the number
of central G-chief factors of such a series. Then α(G) ≤ 4n − 3k.

   The following example shows that the upper bound in Theorem 2 improves
the one in Theorem 1 in some cases.
228                     A. Ballester-Bolinches et al.                 Arch. Math.


Example 1. Let n ≥ 2 and let p1 , p2 , . . . , pn be primes such that p1 < p2 <
· · · < pn . Assume that G1 is a cyclic group of order p1 . For i > 1, deﬁne Gi in-
ductively as the semidirect product Gi = [Vpi ]Gi−1 , where Vpi is a faithful and
irreducible Gi−1 -module over the ﬁeld Fpi of pi elements (such an irreducible
module exists by [6, Corollary B.11.8]). Then
                        1 = G0 ⊂ G1 ⊂ · · · ⊂ Gn = G
is a chief series of G, λ(G) = n, F (G) = Vpn−1 is a minimal normal subgroup
of G and Φ(G) = 1. If n ≥ 5, then α(G) ≤ 4 < n, by Theorem 2.
      Combining Theorems 1 and 2, we have:
Corollary 1. Let G be a soluble group. Assume that n is the length of a G-chief
series of the group F (G)/Φ(G), and k is the number of central G-chief factors
of this series. Then
                         α(G) ≤ min {λ(G), 4n − 3k}.
    Let H/K be a chief factor of a group G. A subgroup A is a complement of
H/K in G if G = AH and A ∩ H = K. We say that H/K is a Frattini chief
factor of G if H/K is contained in the Frattini subgroup of G/K. It is clear
that if H/K is abelian, then H/K is a non-Frattini chief factor of G if and
only if H/K has a complement in G.
    Let δ(G) denote the number of non-Frattini chief factors in a given chief
series of a group G. It is well-known that δ(G) is independent of the choice of
the chief series of G (see [6, Theorem A.9.13]).
    It is noted in [5] that the diﬀerence α(G) − δ(G) can be arbitrarily large.
However, as a consequence of [5, Theorem 4], we have that
                                 α(G) ≤ 4δ(G)
for soluble groups G.
    This bound can be improved with the help of prefrattini subgroups.
    Let Σ be a Hall system of a soluble group G (see [6, Chapter I, Section 1.4]).
By [6, Theorem I.6.6], Σ reduces in exactly one member of every conjugacy
class of maximal subgroups of G. The intersection W of all complements of the
non-Frattini chief factors of G in a given chief series of G into which Σ reduces
is called the prefrattini subgroup of G associated with Σ (see [4, Section 4.3] for
details). According to [9, Theorem 1.1] (see also [3, Corollary 5]), there exist
elements x, y ∈ G such that W ∩ W x ∩ W y = Φ(G). Consequently, we have
                                 α(G) ≤ 3δ(G)
for soluble groups G.
    Our main goal here is to present a new upper bound on the intersection
number of a soluble group in terms of the number of non-Frattini chief factors
of the largest supersoluble quotient of the group.
    Let Φpri (G) be the intersection of all maximal subgroups M of a group G
such that |G : M | is a prime, with the usual convention that Φpri (G) = G if
every maximal subgroup of G has composite index. Furthermore, we denote
by Φcom (G) the intersection of all maximal subgroups of a group G such that
Vol. 125 (2025) On some upper bounds on the intersection number            229


|G : M | is composite (Φcom (G) = G if every maximal subgroup of G has
prime index). This subgroup coincides with the subgroup LU (G) studied in
[2], where U is the saturated formation of all supersoluble groups. According
to [2, Corollary 3.4], Φcom (G) is a supersoluble subgroup of G.
    Note that every group G has a smallest normal subgroup N with supersol-
uble quotient G/N. This subgroup is denoted by GU and is called the super-
soluble residual of the group G.
    We prove the following:
Theorem 3. Let G be a soluble group. Assume that m is the length of the G-
chief series of F (G/Φcom (G)) ∩ (G/Φcom (G))U . Then
                          α(G) ≤ 3δ(G/GU ) + 4m.
   Denote β(G) = 3δ(G/GU ) + 4m, where m is as in Theorem 3. If G is
supersoluble, then GU = 1 and so β(G) = 3δ(G). However, β(G) can be very
much smaller: if G is a group as in Example 1 with p1 not dividing p2 − 1, then
Φcom (G) = 1, GU = Vpn · · · Vp2 and m = 1. Then β(G) = 7 and 3δ(G) = 3n.
Hence β(G) < 3n if n ≥ 3.
   The following example shows that in some cases β(G) is smaller than
min{λ(G), 4n − 3k}, where 4n − 3k is the bound determined in Theorem 2.
Example 2. Let p, q, and r be three primes such that p divides q − 1 and p
does not divide r − 1. Let A be the cyclic group of order pc for some c ≥
1. Let Vq be an irreducible A-module over the ﬁeld of q-elements such that
B = CA (Vq ) is the maximal subgroup of A. Then Vq is one-dimensional. Let
Vr be an irreducible A-module over the ﬁeld of r elements with B = CA (Vr ).
Then Vr is not one-dimensional. Let V be a direct sum of a copies of Vq
and let W be a direct sum of b copies of Vr . Consider G = [V ⊕ W ]A, the
corresponding semidirect product. Then GU = W, F (G) = [V ⊕ W ]B, and
G/GU ∼ = [V ]A. Furthermore, G has a core-free maximal subgroup of composite
index. Therefore Φcom (G) = 1. Hence β(G) = 3a+3+4b, λ(G) = a+b+c, and
the upper bound determined in Theorem 2 is equal to 4a+4b. If we take a = 4,
b = 1, and c = 15, it follows that β(G) = 19, λ(G) = 20, and 4a + 4b = 20.
2. Preliminary results. We begin with an elementary lemma. Its proof is
straightforward.
Lemma 1. Let N be a normal subgroup of a group G.
 (1) If N ⊆ Φpri (G), then Φpri (G/N ) = Φpri (G)/N.
 (2) If N ⊆ Φcom (G), then Φcom (G/N ) = Φcom (G)/N.
 (3) Φ(G/Φcom (G)) = 1.
 (4) Φ(G) = Φpri (G) ∩ Φcom (G).
Lemma 2. If G is a soluble group, then GU ⊆ Φpri (G) and Φpri (G)/GU =
Φ(G/GU ).
Proof. Let M be a maximal subgroup of G such that |G : M | = p, where p is
a prime. Then G/CoreG (M ) is primitive, and since G is soluble, M is a com-
plement of a G-chief factor N/CoreG (M ) in G by [6, Theorem A.15.2]. Since
230                      A. Ballester-Bolinches et al.                   Arch. Math.


|G : M | = |N/CoreG (M )|, it follows that N/CoreG (M ) has order p. By [6,
Theorem A.21.1], G/CG (N/CoreG (M )) is cyclic of order dividing p − 1. Since
CG/CoreG (M ) (N/CoreG (M )) = N/CoreG (M ), we conclude that G/CoreG (M )
is supersoluble. Hence GU ⊆ CoreG (M ) ⊆ M and GU ⊆ Φpri (G).
    Since G/GU is supersoluble, all maximal subgroups of G/GU have prime
index by [6, Theorem VII.2.2]. Hence Φpri (G)/GU =Φpri (G/GU )=Φ(G/GU ).
                                                                           
Lemma 3. Let G be a group. Then α(G) ≤ α(G/Φpri (G)) + α(G/Φcom (G)).
Proof. Suppose that α(G/Φpri (G)) = k. Since Φpri (G/Φpri (G)) = 1 by Lemma 1,
there exist maximal subgroups M1 , M2 , . . . , Mk of G such that, for every
i = 1, 2, . . . , k, |G : Mi | is prime and
                         Φpri (G) = M1 ∩ M2 ∩ · · · ∩ Mk .
Assume that α(G/Φcom (G)) = n. Since Φcom (G/Φcom (G)) = 1 by Lemma 1,
there exist maximal subgroups H1 , H2 , . . . , Hn of G such that, for every j =
1, 2, . . . , n, |G : Hj | is a composite number and
                         Φcom (G) = H1 ∩ H2 ∩ · · · ∩ Hn .
      Then, by Lemma 1, we have
             Φ(G) = (M1 ∩ M2 ∩ · · · ∩ Mk ) ∩ (H1 ∩ H2 ∩ · · · ∩ Hn ).
Hence α(G) = α(G/Φ(G)) ≤ k + n.                                                   
Lemma 4. Let G be a soluble group. Then
                           α(G/Φpri (G)) ≤ δ(G/GU ).
Proof. By Lemma 2, GU ⊆ Φpri (G). Hence G/Φpri (G) is supersoluble. Since
the derived subgroup of every supersoluble group is nilpotent, we can apply
[5, Theorem 4.4] to conclude that α(G/Φpri (G)) ≤ δ(G/GU ).              
Lemma 5 ([7, Theorem 1.4]). Let G be a soluble group and V a finite faithful
G-module. If V is completely reducible, there exist v1 , v2 , v3 ∈ V such that
CG (v1 ) ∩ CG (v2 ) ∩ CG (v3 ) = 1.
      For abelian groups, this can be strengthened as follows.
Lemma 6 ([5, Lemma 4.2]). Let G be an abelian group and let V be a faithful
completely reducible G-module. Then there exists x ∈ V such that CG (x) = 1.
Lemma 7 ([6, Lemma A.16.3]). Let G = [N ]H be a semidirect product of a
normal subgroup N with a subgroup H.
 (a) If n ∈ N, then H ∩ H n = CH (n).
 (b) CoreG (H) = CH (N ).
Lemma 8. Let G be a soluble primitive group. Let M be a maximal subgroup
of G with CoreG (M ) = 1. Then there exist x, y, z ∈ G such that
                            M ∩ M x ∩ M y ∩ M z = 1.
      If G is supersoluble, there exists x ∈ G such that M ∩ M x = 1.
Vol. 125 (2025) On some upper bounds on the intersection number                       231


Proof. Since G is soluble and primitive, G has a unique minimal normal sub-
group N, which is complemented by a maximal subgroup M of G. Moreover,
N = CG (N ) and CoreG (M ) = 1. Hence M acts faithfully and irreducibly on
N.
   By Lemma 5, there exist x, y, z ∈ N such that

                          CM (x) ∩ CM (y) ∩ CM (z) = 1.

Thus, by Lemma 7, we conclude that M ∩ M x ∩ M y ∩ M z = 1.
   If G is supersoluble, then M is abelian. By Lemma 6, there exists x ∈ N
such that CM (x) = 1 and then M ∩ M x = 1.                               

Lemma 9. Let G be a soluble group with Φcom (G) = 1. Suppose that n is the
length of a G-chief series of the group F (G), and k is the number of cyclic
G-chief factors of this series. Then G contains 4n − 2k maximal subgroups
whose intersection is Φcom (G) = 1.

Proof. By Lemma 1, Φ(G) = 1. Then F (G) is a direct product of minimal
normal subgroups of G, all complemented in G by [6, Theorem A.10.6]. Assume
that

                 F (G) = (N1 × · · · × Nk ) × (Nk+1 × · · · × Nn ),

where Ni is a minimal normal subgroup of G of prime order, for all i = 1, . . . , k,
and Nj is a minimal normal subgroup of G of composite order, for every
j ∈ {k + 1, . . . , n}.
   Consider the following G-chief series of F (G):

              1 = N0 ⊂ N1 ⊂ N1 N2 ⊂ · · · ⊂ N1 N2 · · · Nn = F (G).

Assume that Mi is a maximal subgroup of G which complements the G-chief
factor N1 N2 · · · Ni /N1 N2 · · · Ni−1 for each i = 1, . . . , n (N1 N2 . . . Ni−1 = 1 if
i = 1). Let

               X = CoreG (M1 ) ∩ CoreG (M2 ) ∩ · · · ∩ CoreG (Mn ).

   Assume that X = 1 and let N be a minimal normal subgroup of G contained
in X. Then N is contained in F (G), and there exists i ∈ {1, . . . , n} such that
N1 N2 · · · Ni ⊆ N (N1 N2 · · · Ni−1 ). Then G = N Mi . This is impossible since
N ⊆ Mi . Hence X = 1, and

        Φcom (G) = CoreG (M1 ) ∩ CoreG (M2 ) ∩ · · · ∩ CoreG (Mn ) = 1.

By Lemma 8, we have that
                                                x       y       z
                     CoreG (Mj ) = Mj ∩ Mj j ∩ Mj j ∩ Mj j

for every j ∈ {k + 1, . . . , n}, and CoreG (Mi ) = Mi ∩ Mixi for all i = 1, . . . , k.
Hence G contains 4(n−k)+2k = 4n−2k maximal subgroups whose intersection
is Φcom (G) = 1.                                                                     
232                      A. Ballester-Bolinches et al.                  Arch. Math.


3. Proof of Theorem 2.
Proof. We argue by induction on |G|. Assume Φ(G) = 1. Since Φ(G/Φ(G)) = 1
and F (G/Φ(G)) = F (G)/Φ(G), the length of a G/Φ(G)-chief series of the
group F (G/Φ(G)) is equal to n, and the number of central G/Φ(G)-chief
factors of this series is equal to k. By induction, there exist maximal subgroups
M1 /Φ(G), M2 /Φ(G), . . . , M4n−3k /Φ(G) of G/Φ(G) whose intersection is equal
to 1. Then
                       M1 ∩ M2 ∩ . . . ∩ M4n−3k = Φ(G),
and α(G) ≤ 4n − 3k.
   Assume Φ(G) = 1. By [6, Theorem A.10.6], F (G) = N1 · · · Nn is the prod-
uct of minimal normal subgroups N1 , . . . , Nn of G, all complemented in G.
Without loss of generality, we can assume that N1 , N2 , . . . , Nk are central in
G, and Nk+1 , Nk+2 , . . . , Nn are non-central. Consider the G-chief series
             1 = N0 ⊂ N1 ⊂ N1 N2 ⊂ · · · ⊂ N1 N2 · · · Nn = F (G)
of F (G). Assume that Mi is a maximal subgroup of G which complements the
G-chief factor N1 N2 · · · Ni /N1 N2 · · · Ni−1 for each i = 1, . . . , n. Denote the
subgroup
                 CoreG (M1 ) ∩ CoreG (M2 ) ∩ · · · ∩ CoreG (Mn )
by X. As in Lemma 9, we have
       CoreG (M1 ) ∩ CoreG (M2 ) ∩ · · · ∩ CoreG (Mn ) = X = 1 = Φ(G).
By Lemma 8, we have that
                                             x       y      z
                    CoreG (Mj ) = Mj ∩ Mj j ∩ Mj j ∩ Mj j
for every j ∈ {k + 1, . . . , n}. Since the subgroups M1 , M2 , . . . , Mk are normal
in G, CoreG (Mi ) = Mi for every i = 1, 2, . . . , k.
    Hence G contains 4(n − k) + k = 4n − 3k maximal subgroups whose inter-
section is Φ(G). Therefore α(G) ≤ 4n − 3k, as requested.                           
4. Proof of Theorem 3.
Proof. By Lemmas 3 and 4, we have that
   α(G) ≤ α(G/Φpri (G)) + α(G/Φcom (G)) ≤ δ(G/GU ) + α(G/Φcom (G)).
    If (G/Φcom (G))U = 1, then GU is contained in Φ(G) by Lemma 2 and so G
is supersoluble. Hence GU = 1, n = 0, α(G) ≤ 3δ(G), and the theorem holds.
Hence we may assume that (G/Φcom (G))U = 1. Since Φ(G/Φcom (G)) = 1, it
follows that F (G/Φcom (G)) is a direct product of minimal normal subgroups of
G/Φcom (G), all of them complemented in G/Φcom (G) by [6, Theorem A.10.6].
Suppose that N/Φcom (G) is a minimal normal subgroup of G/Φcom (G) con-
tained in (G/Φcom (G))U . By Lemma 1, Φcom (G/Φcom (G)) = 1, and there-
fore there exists a maximal subgroup of G of composite index complement-
ing N/Φcom (G) in G/Φcom (G). In particular, N/Φcom (G) is not cyclic. As-
sume that k is the number of cyclic G-chief factors of a G-chief series of
F (G/Φcom (G)). Since every G-chief factor above GU is cyclic, we conclude that
Vol. 125 (2025) On some upper bounds on the intersection number                     233


m + k is the length of a G-chief series of F (G/Φcom (G)). Applying Lemma 9,
we have that G has 4m+2k maximal subgroups whose intersection is Φcom (G).
In particular, α(G/Φcom (G)) ≤ 4 m + 2k. Therefore
             α(G) = α(G/Φ(G)) ≤ α(G/Φpri (G)) + α(G/Φcom (G))
                      ≤ δ(G/GU ) + 4m + 2k ≤ 3δ(G/GU ) + 4m.
